citing_sentences: Under the default instruction and without tools, GPT-6 Astra recovered the planted relationship in all six runs on the 353-weight networks, including both half-strength versions, with surrogate $R^{2}$ of 0.41–0.88 and no false alarm on the null network (Table 2, Figure 1).

With the calculator, GPT-6 Astra recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs that had one (95% interval 0.88–1.00), on networks of 353 to 38,401 weights, with strength ratios of 0.85–1.10 and surrogate $R^{2}$ of 0.88–0.98 (Table 2, Figure 1).

abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network’s predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.

sections.body: The introduction describes a report that GPT-6 Astra read raw weights of small networks, and critiques that separated tool-free weight reading from code-based analysis. It motivates auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. The authors list their contributions: a factorial evaluation of instruction and access on networks of 105 to 38,401 weights with five models; evidence that tool-free reading works only for small networks; evidence that the default single-reply set-up produced refusals that one paragraph of system instruction removed; and a comparison with scripts that use no language model. All networks, prompts, replies, logs and code are released.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Whether frontier models audit small clinical networks from raw weights or from computation has practical consequences for access.

sections.body: The section reviews three strands. Weight-space programming work reports that GPT-6 Astra read and edited weights, with small networks read from raw weights alone and larger models edited with code. Re-runs reproduced reading of game-playing networks and showed dependence on intact weights, and critics questioned that framing and the mathematics baseline. Automated interpretability agents experiment on systems to explain them; FIND reported that black-box agents captured global behaviour better than local details. The clinical-audit strand notes one study that audited rule-based networks from weights alone, and states that this study adds noisy outcomes, larger sizes and conditions with and without computation.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Earlier work covered weight reading, automated interpretability agents and clinical model audits, each under different access conditions.

sections.body: Table 1 summarises the design. Networks were tanh multilayer perceptrons trained on simulated cohorts of 20,000 adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Each planted relationship was a threshold or an interaction, at full or half strength, or none. Ten neutral laboratory values were added so that medical knowledge could not help. Each run was one prompt and one reply, scored by a script against the ground truth with rules written before the runs. Access was the weights in the prompt with no tools, a calculator exposing the weights (white box), or a calculator exposing only predictions (black box). GPT-6 Astra was the main model. Proportions use Wilson 95% intervals, and the design was adaptive.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Networks trained on simulated cohorts with planted relationships were given to five GPT models under instruction and access conditions, scored by pre-written rules.

sections.body: Without tools, under the default instruction, GPT-6 Astra recovered planted relationships in all six runs on 353-weight networks. At 3,457 weights it recovered the threshold in both runs and the interaction in one of two, and repeats differed widely. Under the default instruction, 11 of 12 audit and repair runs declined (95% interval 0.65–0.99); under the explicit instruction, none of 14 declined (95% interval 0.00–0.22). With the calculator, the planted relationship was recovered in all 29 runs, with strength ratios of 0.85–1.10, and there were no false alarms in 15 null runs. In 18 black-box runs, strength ratios were 0.97–1.10, matching white-box runs. The explicit instruction also had a cost: asked for an exact 1.6 shift, Astra added 0.8 to every patient.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: With tools, GPT-6 Astra recovered planted relationships in all 29 runs up to 38,401 weights, while tool-free reading failed beyond 3,457 weights.

sections.body: The discussion argues that tool-free weight reading and code-assisted analysis behaved very differently, and that performance seems set by the budget for computation and queries rather than by weight visibility. It says a routine audit can run end to end without the model file, although a few lines of script matched the model once the problem was known, and editing weights remained the weakest task. It argues that evaluations should report the instruction and tools used and count refusals separately from wrong answers. The stated limitations: networks were small simulated multilayer perceptrons with hand-set parameters; the models came mainly from one family and one harness; several cells had one to three runs; the scripted search was designed knowing the planted subgroup form; and pre-specification was internal and the design adaptive.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Results come from small simulated networks and one model family, with internal pre-specification and an adaptive design.

sections.body: The conclusion states that without tools, frontier models read small clinical prediction networks from their weights but not larger ones. With a calculation-only tool, they read and audited networks of up to 38,401 weights accurately and stably, and they did as well without seeing the weights. The section says the useful capability for auditing clinical models is automated experimentation, which performed on a par with well-designed scripts in these tests. It closes by saying that any claim about model capability should state how the task was posed and which tools were available.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: With a calculation tool, GPT-6 Astra audited networks of up to 38,401 weights accurately, on a par with well-designed scripts.

sections.body: Appendix A gives, for each experiment, the plan commit, the commit time in UTC+8 and the start of the first run. It lists deviations: up to 14 runs were started at once, causing capacity errors in three runs, and seven batches were stopped and re-queued; empty or JSON-less replies were recorded as declined; the addendum on zero locations and the exact scan were added before affected replies were read; and the description of near misses is post hoc. Appendix B gives the explicit system instruction. Appendix C gives an example reading prompt with the calculator and white-box access, noting that one clause about the training data source was removed from the released prompts.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists pre-specification commits and deviations, the explicit system instruction text, and an example prompt.
